Image-Based Quantification of Amorphous Solid Dispersion Tablet Formulation Disintegration Profiles in a Custom USP-2 Apparatus
works.abstract: Amorphous solid dispersions (ASDs) are single-phase molecular mixtures of amorphous drug and polymer designed to enhance solubility, inhibit crystallization, and improve release rate, increasing bioavailability. During dissolution, water lowers the glass-transition temperature, triggering gelation and polymer chain mobility. This slows erosion compared to that in neat drug systems. Since the tablet surface area controls drug release onset and rate, its quantitative assessment is vital for predicting dissolution and optimizing ASD performance. Traditional methods like United States Pharmacopeia disintegration testing often rely on visual endpoints and may lack sensitivity to formulation nuances. This tool is often being used in the early stages of formulation development, and it is not an efficient testing method for eroding drug product erosion testing. Imaging techniques, such as magnetic resonance imaging and X-ray microtomography (μCT), are resource-intensive, while mass loss tracking is laborious, inefficient, and prone to reproducibility issues. This project introduces a novel image-based disintegration method using a custom USP-2 apparatus with camera monitoring, directly correlating disintegration/erosion mechanisms with dissolution performance. The study includes apparatus design, formulation development, and image analysis. The erosion and dissolution profile of Ritonavir-PVPVA-based ASD (20% drug loading) formulations with different levels of disintegrants, compressed under two different compression forces, were studied with the USP-2 custom-designed device. Erosion was quantified via time-lapse imaging algorithms that segmented tablet boundaries to calculate the longitudinal and transverse surface area profiles. Findings confirm the method's viability for erosion profiling as a robust method for quantifying release mechanisms. Compression force across the range (8-10 kN) revealed negligible influence on erosion, as shown by consistent profiles. The formulation that contained high microcrystalline cellulose (MCC) and no lactose showed swelling, followed by erosion in its release mechanism, while a formulation with low MCC and high lactose exhibited a purely erosion-based release mechanism. This method improves formulation predictability and provides insights for ASD drug product release mechanisms.

works.title: Retraction of “Transferrin-Conjugated Chitosan Nanoparticles for Direct Nose-to-Brain Delivery of Ziprasidone: Pharmacokinetic and Pharmacodynamic Evaluation”
AI-integrated iPSC multi-omics: advancing phenotype discovery and drug target identification in rare diseases
works.abstract: Rare diseases represent a major unmet medical need, yet the development of therapeutics for these diseases is limited by small patient cohorts, fragmented data, and uncertain disease mechanisms. Recent advances that combine patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models with multi-omics profiling and artificial intelligence offer a robust approach for phenotype definition and drug target identification that requires only minimal patient material. By integrating transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic data, machine learning can produce disease-relevant molecular signatures, identify convergent pathway drivers, and prioritize druggable targets despite limited sample sizes. This short review highlights emerging in vitro models and AI-enabled workflows, discusses their strengths and limitations, and outlines practical strategies to accelerate drug discovery for rare diseases.

works.title: CRISPR screens identify ACSL4 as a key regulator in macrophage activation and metabolic inflammation
works.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Pro-inflammatory macrophages drive obesity-associated metabolic inflammation. Identifying key regulators of their activation is crucial for new therapies. This study aimed to identify novel regulators of pro-inflammatory adipose tissue macrophage (ATM) activation and assess their therapeutic potential. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: ) and shRNA-mediated knockdown in macrophage cell lines (RAW264.7, THP-1, and iBMDM). Mechanisms were explored via mutagenesis, immunostaining, co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP), bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC), and transcriptional activity assays. A high-throughput screen of 8,685 DrugBank compounds was performed to identify candidates targeting ACSL4. KEY RESULTS: ACSL4 deficiency markedly reduced pro-inflammatory factor expression (Tnfα, Il1β, and Il6). Myeloid ACSL4 deletion protected against high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity, correlated with reduced pro-inflammatory ATMs and enhanced adipocyte lipolysis and thermogenesis, without affecting food intake, water intake, or locomotor activity in mice. However, glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity were not significantly affected. Mechanistically, ACSL4 contributed to inflammation independent of its enzymatic/ferroptotic functions (Thr328 mutation, troglitazone insensitivity). Instead, ACSL4 translocated to the nucleus in a karyopherin β1 (KPNB1)-dependent manner. DrugBank screening identified abemaciclib as a potential inhibitor of the ACSL4-KPNB1 interaction. Notably, abemaciclib treatment reduced macrophage inflammation and attenuated HFD-induced obesity in mice. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: ACSL4 promotes pro-inflammatory macrophage activation through its KPNB1-dependent nuclear translocation and cooperation with IRF5. Targeting the ACSL4-KPNB1 interaction may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for metabolic inflammation.

works.title: Investigation of the mechanisms and modulation of irinotecan‐induced emesis in Suncus murinus
works.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Irinotecan is a widely used chemotherapeutic agent that frequently causes nausea and emesis. Its emetic mechanism of action is poorly understood and the choice of drugs to reduce nausea and emesis is largely empirical. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Using Suncus murinus, we examined (i) the dose-response and temporal profile of irinotecan-induced emesis; (ii) emetic potential of its active metabolite, SN-38; (iii) involvement of vagal and central pathways; (iv) efficacies of classical antiemetics administered alone, or in combinations. Behavioural, respiratory, metabolic and c-Fos immunohistochemical analyses were used to delineate mechanisms involved in emesis control. A microelectrode array (MEA) system assessed the effects of irinotecan and SN-38 on gastrointestinal slow-wave activity. KEY RESULTS: Irinotecan induced dose-dependent emesis within 24 h, whereas SN-38 was inactive. Neither compound altered respiration. Bilateral abdominal vagotomy attenuated early-phase (0-4 h) of irinotecan-induced emesis. Palonosetron suppressed emesis and was the most effective monotherapy; olanzapine alone also showed antiemetic efficacy. Notably, olanzapine-containing combinations with palonosetron and aprepitant or dexamethasone provided superior protection compared with monotherapies. Irinotecan increased c-Fos expression in the brainstem, and hypothalamic and limbic regions; palonosetron selectively reduced brainstem activation. Serum metabolomics revealed reduced tyramine levels and associations between emetic episodes and 5-HT-related pathways. MEA recordings showed that irinotecan, but not SN-38, produced selective disruptions of upper-gut rhythmic activity. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: Irinotecan-induced emesis is mediated predominantly through 5-HT₃-dependent vagal-brainstem pathways with additional activation of hypothalamic and limbic regions. Altered intestinal pacemaker activity and 5-HT metabolism may contribute to gastrointestinal adverse effects.

works.title: Maternal immunization with RSV-VLPs in a non-human primate model of RSV infection
works.abstract: Using a non-human primate model, we evaluated an RSV pre-fusion F and G protein virus-like particle-based maternal immunization strategy and evaluated the effects of pregnancy on vaccine-induced immunity against RSV. Immunization during pregnancy induced robust systemic and mucosal IgG and neutralizing antibody titers. Upon post-partum challenge, this vaccination strategy enhanced humoral recall responses and Fc-effector functions, and reduced viral load in dams. Infants born to vaccinated dams had increased levels of RSV antibodies in the plasma and lung mucosa, which were correlated with reduced viral load; these infants also exhibited reduced pulmonary eosinophilia. Interestingly, vaccination during pregnancy was associated with increased post-fusion F responses and NAb titers, and we observed a reduction in viral load following post-partum challenge compared to nonpregnant controls. These results support the potential of a VLP-based maternal immunization strategy and provide insight into vaccine-induced immunity against RSV in pregnant and post-partum adults and infants.

works.title: Immunogenicity and protective efficacy of a recombinant HtsA-SLOdm fusion protein against Group A Streptococcus infection
works.abstract: Group A Streptococcus (GAS) is a major human pathogen responsible for a broad spectrum of diseases, yet no licensed vaccine is currently available. Heme-transfer lipoprotein A (HtsA) and streptolysin O (SLO) are key virulence-associated factors involved in iron acquisition and host cell damage, respectively, making them attractive vaccine targets. Here, we designed and evaluated HtsA-SLOdm, a recombinant fusion protein comprising HtsA and a detoxified mutant of SLO, to assess its immunogenicity and protective efficacy against GAS infection. The fusion protein retained the antigenicity of both components and exhibited negligible hemolytic activity without detectable histopathological toxicity in immunized mice. Immunization with alum-adjuvanted HtsA-SLOdm elicited robust antigen-specific antibody responses, with endpoint IgG titers ranging from 1:312,500 to 1:1,562,500. In a murine skin infection model, HtsA-SLOdm vaccination improved survival, reduced lesion size and bacterial load, and alleviated tissue damage, accompanied by enhanced collagen deposition and angiogenesis. Antisera from immunized mice also mediated opsonophagocytic killing of GAS. Mechanistically, HtsA-SLOdm promoted dendritic cell maturation, B-cell activation, and Th1, Th2, and Th17-associated cytokine responses. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that HtsA-SLOdm induces robust humoral and cellular immunity and confers significant protection against GAS infection, highlighting its potential as a promising candidate for GAS vaccine development.

works.title: One year of Commissioner’s National Priority Vouchers
Structural variant detection across sequencing technologies
works.abstract: Structural variants (SVs) are a major source of genomic diversity, yet their discovery remains challenging due to repetitive genomic contexts, alignment ambiguity and the trade-off between sequencing cost and read length. Here we introduce HitSV, which implements repetitiveness- and signature-density-aware breakpoint recognition coupled with precise haplotype-resolved local assembly, thereby enabling base-resolution SV reconstruction and genotyping in various sequencing technologies. On the HG002 benchmark, HitSV achieved 15-72% (long read), 10-36% (short read) and 12% (hybrid sequencing), respectively, higher genotype F1 scores than state-of-the-art SV callers. Applied to the 1KGP phase 4 cohort, HitSV expanded the SV callset by 31.5%, substantially reshaping allele-frequency landscapes. In a large Chinese long-read cohort, HitSV uncovered tandem-repeat-mobile-element composite arrays as a prevalent, multi-allelic class of complex SVs, highlighting composite repeat architectures as an important and previously underrecognized contributor to human structural variation.

A PTPRO inhibitor Pi mitigates endotoxemia‐induced encephalopathy‐mediated blood–brain barrier disruption through cytoskeletal regulation
works.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Septic encephalopathy (SE) is closely associated with disruption of blood-brain barrier (BBB), resulting in neurological deficits and poor clinical outcomes. Protein tyrosine phosphatase receptor type O (PTPRO) regulates disease states by dephosphorylating membrane-associated proteins and modulating intracellular signalling. Here we have examined the role of PTPRO in regulating BBB permeability and have assessed a PTPRO inhibitor (Pi) in mitigating BBB disruption during endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Genetic and pharmacological approaches, including PTPRO overexpression, knockdown or deficiency and Pi treatment, were used to evaluate endothelial dysfunction in bEND.3 cells, primary mouse brain microvascular endothelial cells and an LPS-induced murine model of endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy. Barrier dysfunction, cytoskeletal remodelling and signalling events were assessed using permeability assays, immunoblotting, immunofluorescence and in vivo BBB leakage analyses. KEY RESULTS: LPS increased PTPRO expression in brain tissue from endotoxemic mice and cerebral endothelial cells. Elevated PTPRO promoted F-actin reorganization, stress fibre formation and intercellular gap formation, whereas Pi treatment or PTPRO silencing attenuated these changes. PTPRO overexpression worsened endothelial barrier dysfunction, while Pi reduced thrombin-induced permeability in bEND.3 cells and wild-type primary endothelial cells. Primary endothelial cells from PTPRO-deficient mice were protected. Mechanistically, PTPRO regulated cytoskeletal dynamics through the ErbB2-Rho-MLC2 pathway. In vivo, Pi treatment and PTPRO deficiency reduced BBB leakage, with limited effects on inflammatory cytokines. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: These findings identify PTPRO as an important regulator of BBB disruption in endotoxemia-associated encephalopathy and support pharmacological targeting of PTPRO as a potential strategy for preserving sepsis-associated BBB injury.

works.title: Genome-wide association study of conjugated pneumococcal vaccine antibody responses in South African infants
works.abstract: Abstract Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines have substantially reduced global mortality, yet the genetic basis of vaccine-induced immunity is unclear. We analysed host genetic determinants of PCV7-induced IgG responses in 1017 South African infants. No genome-wide significant associations were identified, including at the HLA locus. In contrast to protein vaccines, where HLA strongly shapes responses, PCV7 responses appear less constrained by HLA-mediated antigen presentation. This reduced constraint could partially explain their consistent effectiveness across diverse populations.
